title: Lead: why you shoot in front of the target
summary: Why the shot must go in front of a moving target, how actual and perceived lead differ, and how the four lead methods work.

body.html: The shot needs a fraction of a second to reach the target, and in that time the target moves on. So if the gun points straight at a crosser (a target flying across in front of you) and stops there, the shot passes behind it. The gun has to point ahead, so that shot and target meet. That gap is lead, in British English also “forward allowance”.
One crossing target, four methods: the actual lead stays the same, the lead you see changes with the method.
body.heading: Watch how the lead works

body.html: Lead grows with the target’s speed, its distance and its angle. At the same speed and distance, a full crosser needs the most. A target flying straight at or away from the shooter needs almost no sideways lead, though rising and falling targets need vertical lead (above or below).

Real numbers are surprising. For orientation, the actual lead on a crosser at about 20 m is often estimated at about a metre (3–4 feet). Lead grows quickly with distance, even a little faster than the distance itself, because the shot slows down as it flies. So if a far target looks the same distance from your barrels as a near one, the real lead in the air is much bigger.

Actual lead is the real distance in front of the clay in the air. The gap the shooter sees between muzzle and target is perceived lead, also called the “lead picture” or “sight picture”. A metre at 20 m looks like a few centimetres at the muzzle. Which method you use changes this picture. If the barrels move at the target’s speed (maintained lead), you see the whole gap. If they move faster than the target (swing-through), you see only a small gap or none at all. In the split second before the shot leaves, the fast-moving gun travels the rest of the way ahead by itself. With ambush the gun does not move, so you must see a gap even bigger than the actual lead, because the target keeps flying while you react.

Many right-handed shooters feel that a left-to-right crosser needs more lead than a right-to-left one. The real lead is the same; only perception differs. So a coach’s “four feet” describes a picture, not a measurement.

Coaches teach lead through a method: a way of getting the muzzles in front of the target. Four methods are common. For a given target the actual lead is the same with each of them; what changes is the picture you see.

Maintained lead: the muzzles start in front of the target, let it close up to the gap you want, then move at its speed, keeping that gap. Many coaches suggest it for long, predictable targets. More: Maintained lead: get in front, stay in front.

Pull-away: you point the barrels at the target (or just at its front edge), move with it for a moment, then pull smoothly ahead and fire. Many coaches start beginners with it, and it often suits quartering targets (flying at an angle away from or towards you) and rising targets. More: Pull-away: on it, with it, pull away, shoot.

Swing-through: the muzzles start behind, move faster than the target, pass through it and fire as they come out in front. It often suits close, fast and overhead targets. More: Swing-through: from behind, through the bird.
Ambush: the muzzles wait still at a point ahead, and the trigger is pulled before the target reaches that point. It can help on a target seen only briefly. More: Ambush and instinctive shooting.

No method is “more correct” than another. Experienced shooters often choose a method for each target. For a beginner it usually works better to learn one method with a coach first. With all three moving-gun methods the gun keeps moving after the shot; see Follow-through, gun speed and tempo.

notes.html: Coaches give lead in feet, in target widths or as a picture. Translate the unit as it is said: converting “four feet” into metres in the middle of an instruction turns a picture into a measurement.

phrases.en: Forget the real distance — what matters is your picture.
phrases.meaning: Do not think in metres in the air; remember the gap you saw at the muzzle when you hit it.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: The lead was right on that hit; keep the same sight picture.

phrases.en: Same lead on the right-to-left, it only looks different.
phrases.meaning: The real lead is equal in both directions; only perception changes.

key_points.html: Lead exists because the target moves while the shot travels.
More speed, distance and angle mean more lead.
Actual lead is often a metre or more in the air at the target; at the muzzle the picture is only centimetres, because the muzzle is close to the eye.
The method changes the picture: with a moving gun, maintained shows the most and swing-through the least; with ambush (gun still) the gap is even bigger.
Four methods: maintained lead, pull-away, swing-through and ambush; learn one with a coach first.

did_you_know.html: Two shooters can break the same target and describe the lead completely differently: one “sees” a metre, the other half a metre. The difference is in how fast each moves the gun.

quiz.explain: Perceived lead is the picture at the muzzle; actual lead is the real distance in the air and is much larger.

quiz.q: Of the methods with a moving gun, which usually gives the largest perceived lead?
quiz.explain: With maintained lead the gun moves no faster than the target, so nothing is added on its own and you have to see the whole gap. With ambush, where the gun is still, the gap seen is even bigger.

quiz.q: Which target needs almost no sideways lead?
quiz.explain: A straight going-away target has no sideways movement; any lead it needs is vertical.
